title: "Checkpoint I — Foundations, Residual Anatomy, Vertex Splitting, and Bounded Circulations"
subtitle: "Part I Blind Diagnostic Assessment (Chapters 01–04 · Untagged Contest Problems & Failure-Mode Triage)"
---

When you solve an exercise at the end of [Chapter 2](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd) ("Residual Graph Geometry and Cut Edge Classification") or [Chapter 4](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd) ("Flows with Demands and Lower-Bound Circulations"), the chapter heading itself hands you half the solution. Before reading a single word of the problem statement, you already know whether to run Tarjan's SCC algorithm on $G_{f^*}$, split vertices into $v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}$, or introduce super-terminals $S^*, T^*$ for affine slack variables $\tilde{f}(e) = f(e) - l(e)$.

In a live ICPC, NOI, Codeforces, or AtCoder contest, **problems arrive completely untagged**. You are given an English, Chinese, or Japanese narrative, a set of numerical constraints ($N, M, K, V_{\max}$), and a two-second time limit. Your most decisive competitive skill is **blind diagnostic recognition**: translating non-graph surface clues into an algebraic conservation law or cut polynomial, and then compiling that algebra into an exact capacity network without falling into any of the six foundational failure modes (`FM-01`–`FM-06`).

::: {.callout-important title="How to Use This Blind Recognition Checkpoint"}
1. **Zero Visible Chapter or Technique Spoilers**: None of the eight problem headers or statements in Section 2 reveal which chapter (`Ch 01`–`Ch 04`) or which graph gadget applies.
2. **Write Down Your 2-Step Diagnosis Before Peeking**: For each problem (`#193`–`#200`), spend 5–10 minutes on scratch paper answering two questions before opening any dropdown:
   - *Step 1 (Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal)*: What conserved quantity, bottleneck entity, or dual cut decision is hidden in the statement, and why does naive greedy or DP fail?
   - *Step 2 (Intermediate Algebraic Representation)*: What are the decision variables $f(e) \in [l(e), u(e)]$ or cut indicators $x_v \in \{0, 1\}$, and what linear conservation or implication equations do they satisfy?
3. **3-Tier Progressive Unmasking**:
   - Open **Hint 1 (Recognition Trigger)** only if you cannot identify which Part I paradigm (`Ch 01`–`Ch 04`) governs the problem.
   - Open **Hint 2 (Algebraic Intermediate Model)** to verify your equations and variable bounds before drawing vertices and edges.
   - Open **Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution** to check your mechanical graph compilation, hand-trace a small example ($N \le 4$), and audit your code against the broken-gadget counterexamples.
:::

## 1. Rapid-Fire Diagnostic Triage Drills (`FM-01`–`FM-06`)

Before tackling the eight full contest problems in Section 2, test your diagnostic reflexes on six short modelling scenarios. Each scenario either contains a subtle **modelling bug** (`FM-01`–`FM-06`) or asks you to identify the **minimal graph compilation fix**. Formulate your diagnosis before expanding the answer callout.

---

### Drill 1.1 — The Greedy Shortest-Path Deletion Trap

You are given a directed unit-capacity graph $G = (V, E)$ ($N \le 500, M \le 1000$) and asked to find the maximum number of edge-disjoint directed paths from $1$ to $N$. A teammate proposes the following $O(M^2)$ algorithm:

1. Run BFS from $1$ to $N$ to find a shortest directed path $P$.
2. If no path exists, stop and return the count of paths found.
3. Delete all edges of $P$ from $G$ and repeat from Step 1.

Construct a 4-vertex counterexample where this algorithm fails, identify the exact Part I failure mode, and state how the residual graph fixes it.

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.1"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-01` (Greedy Path Deletion without Reverse Residual Cancellation, [Chapter 1](../chapters/ch01-conservation-residual-maxflow-mincut.qmd))**.
- **4-Vertex Counterexample**: Let $V = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ with five directed unit edges: $(1 \to 2)$, $(2 \to 3)$, $(3 \to 4)$, $(1 \to 3)$, and $(2 \to 4)$.
  - Suppose Step 1 finds the 3-edge path $P_1 = (1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4)$ and deletes its three edges.
  - The remaining graph has only $(1 \to 3)$ and $(2 \to 4)$, which are disconnected! The greedy algorithm halts and reports $1$ path, whereas $2$ edge-disjoint paths exist: $(1 \to 2 \to 4)$ and $(1 \to 3 \to 4)$.
- **Exact Residual Fix**: Instead of deleting $(2 \to 3)$, skew-symmetric flow conservation (`Ch 01.2`) sets $c_f(2 \to 3) = 0$ and opens a **backward residual arc** $(3 \to 2)$ with capacity $c_f(3 \to 2) = 1$. The second augmenting path $(1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 4)$ traverses $(3 \to 2)$, which algebraically **cancels** $f(2 \to 3)$ from $1$ back to $0$ and splices the two prefixes and suffixes into $(1 \to 3 \to 4)$ and $(1 \to 2 \to 4)$.
::::

---

### Drill 1.2 — The Saturated-Edge Cut Illusion

After running Dinic's algorithm to completion on a directed network $G = (V, E, c, s, t)$, a contestant wants to list all edges $e = (u \to v)$ that belong to **at least one** minimum $s$-$t$ cut (`可行割边`). They output every original edge $e = (u \to v)$ that is **saturated** ($f^*(e) = c(e)$, i.e., $c_{f^*}(u \to v) = 0$).

Why is saturation insufficient, what is the smallest counterexample, and what exact $O(V + E)$ test on $G_{f^*}$ is required?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.2"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-02` (The Saturated $\implies$ Cut Edge Fallacy, [Chapter 2](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd))**.
- **Counterexample**: Consider $s \xrightarrow{1} u \xrightarrow{1} v \xrightarrow{1} t$ with an alternate parallel bypass $u \xrightarrow{1} w \xrightarrow{1} v$.
  - The maximum $s$-$t$ flow is $1$. Suppose Dinic routes $1$ unit along $s \to u \to v \to t$.
  - Then edge $(u \to v)$ is **saturated** ($f^*(u, v) = 1 = c(u, v)$), yet the total capacity between $u$ and $v$ is $2$ while the minimum cut of the network is $1$ (either $(s \to u)$ or $(v \to t)$).
  - In $G_{f^*}$, the forward bypass $u \xrightarrow{1} w \xrightarrow{1} v$ and the backward arc $v \xrightarrow{1} u$ form a directed residual cycle $u \to w \to v \to u$, so $u$ and $v$ belong to the **same Strongly Connected Component** ($\operatorname{scc}(u) = \operatorname{scc}(v)$) and can never be separated by any minimum cut!
- **Exact Residual SCC Criterion (`[AHOI2009] 最小割` Theorem, `Ch 02.2`)**: Run Tarjan's SCC algorithm on $G_{f^*}$. A saturated edge $e = (u \to v)$ belongs to *at least one* minimum cut iff $\operatorname{scc}(u) \neq \operatorname{scc}(v)$, and belongs to *every* minimum cut iff $\operatorname{scc}(u) = \operatorname{scc}(s) \land \operatorname{scc}(v) = \operatorname{scc}(t)$.
::::

---

### Drill 1.3 — The Unsplit Middle Bottleneck & Undirected Bridge Trap

In a 3-stage matching problem (`Luogu P1402 酒店之王`), each guest $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ must be assigned one compatible room $r \in \{1, \dots, P\}$ and one compatible dish $d \in \{1, \dots, Q\}$. A contestant wires $S \xrightarrow{1} \text{Room}_r \xrightarrow{1} \text{Guest}_i \xrightarrow{1} \text{Dish}_d \xrightarrow{1} T$ using a **single vertex** for $\text{Guest}_i$. Later, on an undirected vertex-cut problem, they split each vertex $v$ into $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}$, and for each undirected edge $\{u, v\}$ they add an undirected capacity-$\infty$ edge between $u_{\text{out}}$ and $v_{\text{in}}$ (i.e., both $u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}}$ and $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}$).

What goes wrong in both constructions?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.3"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-03` (Unsplit Internal Vertex Capacities & Undirected Bridge Short-Circuiting, [Chapter 3](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd))**.
- **Bug 1 (Unsplit Guest Vertex)**: If Guest $i$ likes two available rooms $r_1, r_2$ and two available dishes $d_1, d_2$, a single vertex $\text{Guest}_i$ can absorb $2$ units of flow from $r_1, r_2$ and emit $2$ units to $d_1, d_2$, counting one guest as two satisfied people! Every middle bottleneck entity must be split into $\text{Guest}_{i,\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} \text{Guest}_{i,\text{out}}$.
- **Bug 2 (Reversed $\infty$-Arc on Split Vertices)**: Adding $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}$ allows flow arriving at $v_{\text{in}}$ (say from some $w_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}$) to immediately exit through $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{out}}$ **without ever crossing the internal bottleneck arc $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}$**! An undirected edge $\{u, v\}$ between vertex-split nodes must always be compiled as two **separately directed** $\infty$-bridges:
  $$u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}} \quad \text{and} \quad v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}.$$
::::

---

### Drill 1.4 — The Time-Expanded Infinite Loop & Missing Holdover Bug

In a discrete-time evacuation problem (`Luogu P2754 家园`), $K$ astronauts at station $0$ must reach the Moon ($N+1$) using periodic shuttles. A solver loops $T = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, adding shuttle transit arcs $(u_{t-1}, T-1) \xrightarrow{H_i} (u_t, T)$ and running Dinic from scratch at each step $T$ until $\text{MaxFlow} \ge K$. However, they do not add arcs $(v, T-1) \to (v, T)$ for stations $v$, and their code gets `Time Limit Exceeded` on an instance where the Moon is unreachable.

Identify all three defects in this time-expanded compilation.

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.4"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-04` (Time-Expanded Horizon Traps, [Chapter 3](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd))**.
- **Three Required Fixes**:
  1. **Missing Station Holdover Arcs**: Without $(v, T-1) \xrightarrow{\infty} (v, T)$, astronauts who disembark at station $v$ at time $T-1$ vanish unless another shuttle leaves $v$ at the exact same instant! Holdover arcs allow inventory/passengers to wait at station $v$ across time steps.
  2. **Unchecked Unreachability (`Infinite Loop`)**: Before starting the incremental time loop $T = 1, 2, \dots$, you must verify via DSU or BFS on the static union of shuttle routes whether $0 \leadsto N+1$ is reachable at all.
  3. **Rebuilding Dinic from Scratch**: Because adding layer $T$ only appends new vertices and forward arcs to an existing network, you should keep the **persistent residual network** $G_{f_{T-1}}$ and call `dinic(S, T_sink)` incrementally to augment only the newly unlocked flow!
::::

---

### Drill 1.5 — The Feedback-Arc Leakage Bug in Bounded $s$-$t$ Max-Flow

To solve a Maximum $s$-$t$ Flow problem with edge lower bounds $l(e) \le f(e) \le u(e)$, a contestant adds the feedback arc $e_{\text{fb}} = (t \to s, [0, \infty))$, computes $M(v) = \text{in}_l(v) - \text{out}_l(v)$, and runs Phase 1 `dinic(S*, T*)`. After verifying that Phase 1 saturates $\Sigma^+$, they read off $f_0 = \tilde{f}(t \to s)$ and immediately call Phase 2 `dinic(s, t)` on the residual network without modifying $e_{\text{fb}}$. Their Phase 2 call returns $\infty$. Why?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.5"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-05` (Feedback-Arc Leakage & Slack Offset Omission, [Chapter 4](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd))**.
- **Why Phase 2 Returns $\infty$**: In the residual network after Phase 1, the feedback arc $t \to s$ has residual capacity $\infty - f_0 = \infty$, and its reverse companion arc $s \to t$ has residual capacity $f_0$! Worse, if any $s \leadsto t$ path exists, or directly along the reverse residual arc $s \xrightarrow{f_0} t$, Phase 2 interacts with the artificial feedback edge. Specifically, if you leave the reverse residual arc $s \to t$ active (or if you run `dinic(t, s)` for minimum flow while $t \xrightarrow{\infty} s$ is still open), flow circulates around the artificial feedback loop!
- **Exact Protocol (`Ch 04.2`)**: After recording $f_0 = \tilde{f}(t \to s) = \text{cap}[e_{\text{fb}} \oplus 1]$, you **must zero out both half-edges** of the feedback arc (`cap[e_fb] = cap[e_fb ^ 1] = 0`) before calling Phase 2 `dinic(s, t)` (for $F_{\max} = f_0 + \Delta^+$) or `dinic(t, s)` (for $F_{\min} = f_0 - \Delta^-$). Finally, reconstruct each edge's physical flow as $f(e) = l(e) + \tilde{f}(e)$.
::::

---

### Drill 1.6 — The Mixed-Graph Eulerian Orientation Trap

You are given a connected mixed graph $G = (V, E_{\text{dir}} \sqcup E_{\text{undir}})$ (`POJ 1637 Sightseeing Tour`) and asked whether every undirected edge can be oriented so the resulting directed graph has an Eulerian circuit ($\text{in}(v) = \text{out}(v)$ for all $v \in V$). A solver arbitrarily orients each undirected edge as $u \to v$, computes $D(v) = \text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)$, wires $S \xrightarrow{D(v)} v$ (for $D(v) > 0$) and $v \xrightarrow{-D(v)} T$ (for $D(v) < 0$), and puts capacity $1$ on each reversible edge $u \to v$.

Why does this fail even on a single 2-vertex, 2-edge graph?

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer & Diagnosis — Drill 1.6"}
- **Failure Mode**: **`FM-06` (Mixed Eulerian Parity Omission & Unit-vs-Two Delta Bug, [Chapter 4](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd))**.
- **Two Compounding Bugs**:
  1. **Each Reversal Changes $\text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)$ by $2$, Not $1$**: When an initially oriented edge $u \to v$ is reversed to $v \to u$, $\text{out}(u)$ decreases by $1$ and $\text{in}(u)$ increases by $1$, so $D(u) = \text{in}(u) - \text{out}(u)$ changes by $+2$ (and $D(v)$ changes by $-2$).
  2. **Mandatory Parity Pre-Check**: Because every reversal changes $D(v)$ by $\pm 2$, a valid orientation is **immediately impossible** if any vertex $v \in V$ has $D(v) \not\equiv 0 \pmod 2$ (equivalently, if the total degree $\deg(v)$ is odd)!
- **Exact Compilation (`Ch 04.3`)**: First check that $D(v) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ for all $v \in V$. Then divide by $2$: wire $S \xrightarrow{-D(v)/2} v$ when $D(v) < 0$ (excess out-degree) and $v \xrightarrow{D(v)/2} T$ when $D(v) > 0$ (excess in-degree), with unit capacity $1$ on each reversible undirected arc $u \to v$, and check if $\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) = \sum_{D(v) > 0} D(v)/2$.
::::

## 2. Blind Checkpoint Problems (`#193`–`#200`)

The following eight problems span the full toolkit of Part I (`Ch 01`–`Ch 04`). Remember: **read the statement, inspect the constraints, and write down your Step 1 (Diagnostic Signal) and Step 2 (Algebraic Model) before opening Hint 1.**

---

### Problem `#193` — CSES 1711: Distinct Routes (`[EN]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1711](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1711)
- **Constraints**: $2 \le N \le 500$ rooms, $1 \le M \le 1000$ one-way teleporters, Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  A game consists of $N$ rooms and $M$ one-way teleporters between rooms. You start in room $1$ and must reach room $N$ each day. Every teleporter $e = (u \to v)$ can be used **at most once** across the entire game. Determine the maximum number of days $K$ you can play, and **explicitly output the room sequence of each of the $K$ routes**.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal)"}
- **Target Chapter**: **[Chapter 1](../chapters/ch01-conservation-residual-maxflow-mincut.qmd) (`§1.4` Flow Decomposition Theorem & Menger's Edge-Disjoint Connectivity)**.
- **Diagnostic Clue**: "Each directed teleporter used at most once" + "maximize the number of $1 \leadsto N$ routes and print them." As we saw in Drill 1.1 (`FM-01`), greedily extracting shortest paths fails because an early path can straddle a bridge edge and block two disjoint paths. You must first compute the global maximum unit flow $f^*$, and only *after* all residual cancellations have settled, decompose $f^*$ into $K = |f^*|$ directed $1 \leadsto N$ paths.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model"}
For each teleporter $e = (u \to v) \in E$, introduce a binary flow variable $f(e) \in \{0, 1\}$. Enforce Kirchhoff nodal conservation at every interior room:

$$\sum_{e \in \delta^+(v)} f(e) - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(v)} f(e) = 0 \qquad \forall v \in \{2, \dots, N-1\}$$

and maximize $|f| = \sum_{e \in \delta^+(1)} f(e) - \sum_{e \in \delta^-(1)} f(e)$. By the **Flow Decomposition Theorem (`Ch 01.4`)**, any integral $1$-$N$ flow $f^*$ with $f^*(e) \in \{0, 1\}$ is the edge-disjoint sum of $K = |f^*|$ directed $1 \leadsto N$ paths and zero or more directed cycles.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #193 (CSES 1711)"}

#### Step 1 & Step 2: Recognition & Algebraic Formulation
Each teleporter $e = (u \to v)$ has capacity $c(e) = 1$. In any converged integral maximum flow $f^*$, an original forward teleporter $e = (u \to v)$ is active ($f^*(e) = 1$) if and only if its forward residual capacity is $c_{f^*}(u \to v) = 0$ (equivalently, its companion backward arc $v \to u$ has residual capacity $1$).

#### Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation & Path Extraction Contract
1. **Network Construction**: Create vertices $1, \dots, N$. For each input teleporter $(u, v)$, add a directed arc $u \xrightarrow{1} v$ (keeping a flag or checking `edge_idx % 2 == 0` to distinguish original forward arcs from synthetic reverse residual arcs).
2. **Blocking-Flow Solve**: Run `K = dinic(1, N)`. By Dinic's unit-capacity complexity theorem (`Ch 01.3`), this takes $O(M \min(N^{2/3}, M^{1/2})) \le 3 \cdot 10^4$ operations.
3. **Constructive Path Peeling (`Ch 01.4`)**:
   - Consider the subgraph $E_{\text{active}} = \{e = (u \to v) \in E : f^*(e) = 1\}$. At every interior vertex $v \notin \{1, N\}$, $\deg^+_{\text{active}}(v) = \deg^-_{\text{active}}(v)$, while $\deg^+_{\text{active}}(1) - \deg^-_{\text{active}}(1) = K$.
   - Repeat $K$ times: start at $u = 1$, and greedily follow any active original forward arc $e = (u \to v)$ with $f^*(e) = 1$, immediately setting $f^*(e) \gets 0$ (marking it consumed) until reaching $N$.
   - *Subtlety (What if $E_{\text{active}}$ contains a directed cycle?)*: In a unit network solved by Dinic from $f \equiv 0$, augmenting along shortest level-graph paths rarely creates isolated flow cycles, **but** if a vertex $v$ on the current walk has both an $s \leadsto t$ path and a directed cycle through $v$, a naive walk that enters the cycle simply loops back to $v$ and then continues to $N$! To print strictly **simple** paths (or avoid any dead-end if a cycle touches $1$), either run a standard Eulerian/DFS post-order walk that splices out cycles, or walk $1 \leadsto N$ via DFS and only record the simple stack path when $N$ is reached.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit
- **Toy Trace ($N = 4, M = 5$)**: Edges $e_1=(1\to 2), e_2=(2\to 3), e_3=(3\to 4), e_4=(1\to 3), e_5=(2\to 4)$.
  - Augmentation 1 pushes $1$ unit along $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4$. Now $c_f(2\to 3)=0$ and reverse arc $c_f(3\to 2)=1$.
  - Augmentation 2 pushes $1$ unit along $1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 4$, traversing the reverse arc $3 \to 2$.
  - After Dinic terminates ($K = 2$), check original forward arcs with $c_{f^*}(e) = 0$: they are $e_1(1\to 2), e_3(3\to 4), e_4(1\to 3), e_5(2\to 4)$—notice $e_2(2\to 3)$ now has $c_{f^*}(2\to 3) = 1$ ($f^*(2\to 3) = 0$)!
  - Peeling $2$ paths from $E_{\text{active}}$ yields `1 -> 2 -> 4` (length 3) and `1 -> 3 -> 4` (length 3).
- **Broken-Gadget Warning**: When scanning the adjacency list during path reconstruction, **never allow the walk to traverse odd-indexed reverse residual arcs**! A reverse residual arc $3 \to 2$ with $c_{f^*}(3\to 2) = 0$ just means the forward arc $2 \to 3$ is unused ($f^*(2\to 3) = 0$). Only original forward arcs (`id % 2 == 0` with `cap[id] == 0`) represent physical teleporters used in the solution.
- **Complexity**: Time $O(M\sqrt{N} + K \cdot N)$, Space $O(N + M)$.
::::

### Problem `#194` — Luogu P1345: `[USACO 5.4]` Telecowmunication (`奶牛的电信`, `[EN]`/`[ZH]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P1345](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P1345)
- **Constraints**: $2 \le N \le 100$ computers, $1 \le M \le 600$ bidirectional cables, two distinct hub computers $c_1, c_2 \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  Farmer John's $N$ computers are connected by $M$ bidirectional cables so that data can travel between any two computers through a sequence of intermediate computers. An accident may destroy some computers (together with all cables attached to them), but **cables themselves never fail on their own**, and the two endpoint computers $c_1$ and $c_2$ can never be destroyed. Find the minimum number of computers that must be destroyed so that $c_1$ and $c_2$ can no longer communicate.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal)"}
- **Target Chapter**: **[Chapter 3](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd) (`§3.1` Internal Vertex Capacity Splitting $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c(v)} v_{\text{out}}$ & Vertex-Disjoint Menger Duality)**.
- **Diagnostic Clue**: "Cables never fail; computers fail." We are looking for a **Minimum $c_1$-$c_2$ Vertex Cut** on an undirected graph. Standard edge-cut capacities on the original graph fail because destroying one degree-$d$ computer simultaneously breaks all $\binom{d}{2}$ pairs of paths passing through it at a single unit cost of $1$.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model"}
By Menger's Vertex-Connectivity Theorem (`Ch 03.1`), the minimum number of intermediate vertices whose removal disconnects $c_1$ from $c_2$ equals the maximum number of **internally vertex-disjoint** paths between $c_1$ and $c_2$. Split every computer $v \in V$ into an entry port $v_{\text{in}}$ and an exit port $v_{\text{out}}$ with cut indicators $x_{v,\text{in}}, x_{v,\text{out}} \in \{0, 1\}$:
- Destroying computer $v \notin \{c_1, c_2\}$ corresponds to placing $v_{\text{in}} \in S$ ($x_{v,\text{in}} = 1$) and $v_{\text{out}} \in T$ ($x_{v,\text{out}} = 0$) at cost $1$.
- An invulnerable bidirectional cable $\{u, v\}$ forbids both $(u_{\text{out}} \in S \land v_{\text{in}} \in T)$ and $(v_{\text{out}} \in S \land u_{\text{in}} \in T)$ at cost $\infty$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #194 (Luogu P1345)"}

#### Step 1 & Step 2: Recognition & Algebraic Formulation
Let each vertex $v \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ be mapped to $v_{\text{in}} = v$ and $v_{\text{out}} = v + N$ in a $2N$-vertex directed network. In the primal flow view, any path visiting $v$ must enter $v_{\text{in}}$, traverse the internal bridge $v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}$, and leave from $v_{\text{out}}$. Setting the capacity of $v_{\text{in}} \to v_{\text{out}}$ to $1$ limits vertex $v$ to at most $1$ unit of throughput.

#### Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation
1. **Internal Vertex Arcs**:
   - For each $v \in \{1, \dots, N\} \setminus \{c_1, c_2\}$, add a directed arc $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}$.
   - For $v \in \{c_1, c_2\}$, either add $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{out}}$ or directly set the flow source to $S = (c_1)_{\text{out}}$ and the flow sink to $T = (c_2)_{\text{in}}$.
2. **Bidirectional Cable Arcs**:
   - For each undirected cable $\{u, v\}$, add **two separate directed $\infty$-arcs**:
     $$u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} v_{\text{in}} \quad \text{and} \quad v_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}.$$
3. **Solve**: Output `dinic(c1 + N, c2)`. Since every internal vertex has unit capacity (`Ch 01.3` Unit-Vertex Regime), Dinic runs in $O(M \sqrt{N})$ time.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit
- **Toy Trace ($N = 4$, $c_1 = 1, c_2 = 4$, cables $\{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}, \{2,4\}, \{3,4\}$)**:
  - Vertices $2$ and $3$ have internal arcs $2_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 2_{\text{out}}$ and $3_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} 3_{\text{out}}$.
  - Path 1 routes $1_{\text{out}} \to 2_{\text{in}} \to 2_{\text{out}} \to 4_{\text{in}}$ (saturating $2_{\text{in}} \to 2_{\text{out}}$).
  - Path 2 routes $1_{\text{out}} \to 3_{\text{in}} \to 3_{\text{out}} \to 4_{\text{in}}$ (saturating $3_{\text{in}} \to 3_{\text{out}}$).
  - Total flow $= 2$, matching the minimum vertex cut $\{2, 3\}$.
- **Broken-Gadget Warning (`FM-03`)**: Never compile the undirected cable $\{u, v\}$ by giving the reverse residual arc of $u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}$ an initial capacity of $\infty$! The reverse residual arc of $u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}$ goes from $v_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}$; if it starts with positive capacity, flow entering $v_{\text{in}}$ from $1_{\text{out}}$ can immediately escape to $u_{\text{out}}$ without ever passing through $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} v_{\text{out}}$! You must create two distinct directed edges: $(u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}, \text{cap}=\infty, \text{rev\_cap}=0)$ and $(v_{\text{out}} \to u_{\text{in}}, \text{cap}=\infty, \text{rev\_cap}=0)$.
- **Complexity**: Time $O(M\sqrt{N})$, Space $O(N + M)$.
::::

### Problem `#195` — Luogu P2763: 试题库问题 (`网络流 24 题 #07`, `[ZH]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2763](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2763)
- **Constraints**: $2 \le K \le 20$ categories, $K \le N \le 1000$ problems in the bank, total required problems $M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j \le N$, Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  An exam paper must be assembled from a test bank of $N$ problems spanning $K$ categories. Category $j \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ requires **exactly $c_j$ problems**, so the exam contains $M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j$ problems in total. Each problem $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ is tagged with a subset of categories $S_i \subseteq \{1, \dots, K\}$ to which it belongs. A problem may be included on the exam **at most once**, and if included, it can count toward **only one** of the categories in $S_i$. Determine whether a valid exam paper can be assembled; if so, output the exact list of problem IDs assigned to each category $j = 1, \dots, K$, or print `No Solution!` otherwise.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal)"}
- **Target Chapter**: **[Chapter 1](../chapters/ch01-conservation-residual-maxflow-mincut.qmd) (`§1.1` Supply-Demand Quota Conservation) & [Chapter 3](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd) (`§3.3` Rank-2 Binary Constraint Factorization)**.
- **Diagnostic Clue**: Every individual selection decision ("assign problem $i$ to category $j \in S_i$") simultaneously consumes $1$ unit from problem $i$'s usage limit ($\le 1$) and $1$ unit from category $j$'s quota ($= c_j$). Whenever each decision touches **at most two constraint families** (one Problem and one Category), the constraint matrix is a bipartite incidence matrix!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model"}
Introduce binary decision variables $f_{i, j} \in \{0, 1\}$ for each $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ and $j \in S_i$:

$$\sum_{j \in S_i} f_{i, j} \le 1 \quad (\forall i \in \{1, \dots, N\}), \qquad \sum_{i : j \in S_i} f_{i, j} = c_j \quad (\forall j \in \{1, \dots, K\}).$$

Relaxing $\sum_{i : j \in S_i} f_{i, j} = c_j$ to $\le c_j$ and maximizing $\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j \in S_i} f_{i, j}$ achieves value $M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j$ if and only if all $K$ category quotas are simultaneously met with equality.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #195 (Luogu P2763)"}

#### Step 1 & Step 2: Recognition & Algebraic Formulation
Why does greedy assignment fail? If Problem 1 has tags $\{A, B\}$, Problem 2 has tag $\{A\}$, and Categories $A, B$ each need $1$ problem, greedily assigning Problem 1 to Category $A$ leaves Category $B$ starved; residual cancellation is required to reroute Problem 1 to $B$ and Problem 2 to $A$.

#### Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation & Assignment Recovery
1. **Vertices**: Source $S = 0$, Problem nodes $\text{Prob}_i = i$ ($i = 1, \dots, N$), Category nodes $\text{Cat}_j = N + j$ ($j = 1, \dots, K$), and Sink $T = N + K + 1$.
2. **Directed Arcs**:
   - **Per-Problem Single-Use Cap**: $S \xrightarrow{1} \text{Prob}_i$ for each $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$.
   - **Tag Compatibility Bridges**: $\text{Prob}_i \xrightarrow{1} \text{Cat}_j$ for each $j \in S_i$.
   - **Category Quotas**: $\text{Cat}_j \xrightarrow{c_j} T$ for each $j \in \{1, \dots, K\}$.
3. **Feasibility Check & Residual Extraction**:
   - Compute $F^* = \text{dinic}(S, T)$.
   - If $F^* < M = \sum_{j=1}^K c_j$, output `No Solution!`.
   - Otherwise, for each category $j = 1, \dots, K$, iterate over all incident arcs connecting $\text{Cat}_j$ to $\text{Prob}_i$: whenever the forward arc $\text{Prob}_i \to \text{Cat}_j$ is saturated (`cap == 0`, i.e., its companion reverse arc $\text{Cat}_j \to \text{Prob}_i$ has residual capacity $1$), append $i$ to category $j$'s output list.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit
- **Toy Trace ($N = 3, K = 2, c_1 = 1, c_2 = 1$, $S_1 = \{1, 2\}, S_2 = \{1\}, S_3 = \emptyset$)**:
  - Path 1 pushes $S \to \text{Prob}_1 \to \text{Cat}_1 \to T$.
  - Path 2 pushes $S \to \text{Prob}_2 \to \text{Cat}_1 \xrightarrow{\text{rev}} \text{Prob}_1 \to \text{Cat}_2 \to T$, using the reverse residual arc $\text{Cat}_1 \to \text{Prob}_1$ to reassign $\text{Prob}_1$ from Category 1 to Category 2!
  - Final saturated bridges: $\text{Prob}_2 \to \text{Cat}_1$ and $\text{Prob}_1 \to \text{Cat}_2$.
- **Broken-Gadget Warning**: Never omit the capacity-$1$ bound on $S \to \text{Prob}_i$ (or set it to $|S_i|$)! If $S \to \text{Prob}_i$ had capacity $> 1$, a single multi-tagged problem $i$ would be duplicated across several categories on the same exam paper.
- **Complexity**: Since every $\text{Prob}_i$ has in-degree $1$ of capacity $1$, the network is a **unit-vertex network** (`Ch 01.3`), so Dinic runs in $O(NK \sqrt{N + K})$ time and $O(NK)$ space.
::::

### Problem `#196` — AtCoder ARC 074 D (F — Lotus Leaves, `[JA]`)

- **Judge URL**: [https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc074/tasks/arc074_d](https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc074/tasks/arc074_d)
- **Constraints**: $2 \le H, W \le 100$, grid characters in `{'S', 'T', 'o', '.'}`, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Untagged Problem Statement**:
  There is a pond Represented as an $H \times W$ grid. Cell $(r, c)$ contains either the starting lotus leaf `'S'`, the destination lotus leaf `'T'`, an intermediate lotus leaf `'o'`, or water `'.'`. A frog starts on `'S'` and can jump between any two lotus leaves that lie in the **same row** or the **same column** (regardless of water or other leaves in between). Find the minimum number of `'o'` leaves you must remove so that the frog can no longer reach `'T'` from `'S'`, or output `-1` if `'T'` remains reachable even after removing all `'o'` leaves.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Recognition Trigger (Chapter & Paradigm Reveal)"}
- **Target Chapter**: **[Chapter 3](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd) (`§3.1` Vertex Splitting + `§3.3` Row/Column Hub Virtualization)**.
- **Diagnostic Clue**: If `'S'` and `'T'` share the same row ($r_S = r_T$) or the same column ($c_S = c_T$), the frog jumps directly in $1$ step and the answer is `-1`. Otherwise, we want a Minimum Vertex Cut of `'o'` leaves. However, connecting every pair of leaves in the same row or column directly creates $O(HW(H + W)) \approx 2 \cdot 10^6$ edges on $2HW \approx 2 \cdot 10^4$ split vertices! Instead, observe that jumping within row $r$ or column $c$ means **Row $r$ and Column $c$ act as zero-cost transit hubs (`Ch 03.3`)**!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Algebraic Intermediate Model"}
Assign a binary reachability indicator $x_{R_r} \in \{0, 1\}$ to each Row $r \in \{1, \dots, H\}$ and $x_{C_c} \in \{0, 1\}$ to each Column $c \in \{1, \dots, W\}$:
- Starting on `'S'` at $(r_S, c_S)$ immediately makes Row $r_S$ and Column $c_S$ reachable: $x_{R_{r_S}} = x_{C_{c_S}} = 1$.
- For `'T'` at $(r_T, c_T)$ to be unreachable, neither Row $r_T$ nor Column $c_T$ may be reachable: $x_{R_{r_T}} = x_{C_{c_T}} = 0$.
- Stepping onto an intact leaf `'o'` at $(r, c)$ allows the frog to switch from Row $r$ to Column $c$ **or** from Column $c$ to Row $r$. Thus, leaf $(r, c)$ must be deleted (at cost $1$) whenever $x_{R_r} \neq x_{C_c}$:
  $$\text{Cost of leaf } (r, c) = 1 \cdot [x_{R_r} = 1 \land x_{C_c} = 0] + 1 \cdot [x_{C_c} = 1 \land x_{R_r} = 0] = |x_{R_r} - x_{C_c}|.$$
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Problem #196 (ARC 074 D / F)"}

#### Step 1 & Step 2: From $O(HW(H+W))$ Clique Edges to a $200$-Vertex Bipartite Hub Cut
Let us see how both the **Explicit Vertex-Split View (`Ch 03.1`)** and the **Contracted Row-Column Hub View (`Ch 03.3`)** produce the exact same network:
- *View A (Explicit Leaf Splitting)*: Create row hubs $R_1, \dots, R_H$ and column hubs $C_1, \dots, C_W$. Split each leaf `'o'` at $(r, c)$ into $\ell_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} \ell_{\text{out}}$, and wire $\infty$-edges $R_r \xrightarrow{\infty} \ell_{\text{in}}, C_c \xrightarrow{\infty} \ell_{\text{in}}$ and $\ell_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} R_r, \ell_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} C_c$.
- *View B (Algebraic Contraction to Row/Column Hubs)*: Notice that in View A, $\ell_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1} \ell_{\text{out}}$ is simply a unit-capacity switch between $R_r$ and $C_c$! Because any $s$-$t$ cut places $(R_r, C_c)$ in one of the four states $(S, S), (T, T), (S, T), (T, S)$, replacing the 2-node gadget $(\ell_{\text{in}}, \ell_{\text{out}})$ with a single **undirected unit-capacity edge** $R_r \xleftrightarrow{1} C_c$ (i.e., $R_r \xrightarrow{1} C_c$ and $C_c \xrightarrow{1} R_r$) assigns cut cost $0$ when $x_{R_r} = x_{C_c}$ and cut cost $1$ when $x_{R_r} \neq x_{C_c}$! This shrinks the entire graph from $2HW + H + W \approx 20{,}200$ vertices down to **$H + W + 2 \le 202$ vertices**!

#### Step 3: Mechanical Graph Compilation
1. **Direct-Jump Guard**: Locate `'S'` at $(r_S, c_S)$ and `'T'` at $(r_T, c_T)$. If $r_S == r_T$ or $c_S == c_T$, output `-1` and terminate.
2. **Vertices**: Source $S_{\text{src}} = 0$, Row hubs $R_1, \dots, R_H$ ($1 \dots H$), Column hubs $C_1, \dots, C_W$ ($H+1 \dots H+W$), Sink $T_{\text{snk}} = H + W + 1$.
3. **Edges**:
   - Wire $S_{\text{src}} \xrightarrow{\infty} R_{r_S}$ and $S_{\text{src}} \xrightarrow{\infty} C_{c_S}$.
   - Wire $R_{r_T} \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{snk}}$ and $C_{c_T} \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{snk}}$.
   - For every intermediate leaf `'o'` at $(r, c)$, add two directed unit-capacity arcs:
     $$R_r \xrightarrow{1} C_c \quad \text{and} \quad C_c \xrightarrow{1} R_r.$$
4. **Solve**: Output `dinic(S_src, T_snk)`.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Broken-Gadget Audit
- **Toy Trace ($3 \times 3$ pond)**:
  ```text
  S o .
  . o .
  . o T
  ```
  Here `'S'` is at $(1, 1)$, `'T'` is at $(3, 3)$, and `'o'` leaves are at $(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2)$.
  - $S_{\text{src}} \xrightarrow{\infty} R_1, C_1$ and $R_3, C_3 \xrightarrow{\infty} T_{\text{snk}}$.
  - Leaf $(1, 2)$ gives $R_1 \xleftrightarrow{1} C_2$; leaf $(2, 2)$ gives $R_2 \xleftrightarrow{1} C_2$; leaf $(3, 2)$ gives $R_3 \xleftrightarrow{1} C_2$.
  - Unique $S_{\text{src}} \leadsto T_{\text{snk}}$ path is $S_{\text{src}} \to R_1 \xrightarrow{1} C_2 \xrightarrow{1} R_3 \to T_{\text{snk}}$ of capacity $1$ (note leaf $(2, 2)$ is a dead end $C_2 \leftrightarrow R_2$).
  - Minimum cut $= 1$ (deleting either leaf $(1, 2)$ or leaf $(3, 2)$).
- **Broken-Gadget Warning**: What if you orient the leaf edge in only one direction ($R_r \xrightarrow{1} C_c$ without $C_c \xrightarrow{1} R_r$)? Look at the $3 \times 3$ trace above: the frog jumps from `'S'` in Row $1$ to leaf $(1, 2)$ in Column $2$ ($R_1 \to C_2$), and then jumps **along Column $2$** to leaf $(3, 2)$ in Row $3$ ($C_2 \to R_3$), and finally along Row $3$ to `'T'`! If $C_2 \to R_3$ were omitted, the frog could never transition from a column back to a row, falsely reporting a cut of $0$!
- **Complexity**: $|V| = H + W + 2 \le 202$, $|E| \le 2HW + 4 \le 20{,}004$ unit-capacity edges. Dinic runs in $O(HW \sqrt{H + W}) \approx 1.4 \cdot 10^5$ operations ($< 5\text{ ms}$).
::::

### Problem #197 — ZOJ 2587: Unique Attack `[EN]`

- **Judge & Bounds**: [ZOJ 2587](https://zoj.pintia.cn/problem-sets/91827364500/problems/91827366086) · $N \le 800$ vertices, $M \le 10^4$ undirected communication links with positive integer disruption costs $w_e \ge 1$, source terminal $A$, sink terminal $B$.
- **Untagged Statement**: A saboteur wants to disconnect terminal $A$ from terminal $B$ in an undirected network by severing a subset of links of minimum total disruption cost. Determine whether the set of links severed in a minimum-cost disconnection is **strictly unique** — that is, whether there exists only one subset of edges whose removal disconnects $A$ from $B$ at the minimum possible total cost. Output `"UNIQUE"` or `"AMBIGUOUS"`.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#197)"}

- **Target Chapter & Archetype**: [Ch 02 — Residual Graph Anatomy, Minimum-Cut Structure & Dynamic Edge Updates](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd) (`§2.1` Extremal Minimum Cuts $S_{\min}$ vs. $S_{\max}$ and the Submodular Cut Lattice).
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Asking whether the minimum $A$-$B$ cut is *unique* ($N \le 800, M \le 10^4$) cannot be answered by checking whether each individual cut edge is saturated, nor by re-running Dinic $M$ times. You must inspect the **distributive lattice of all minimum cuts** inside the final residual graph $G_{f^*}$ using a single forward reachability pass from $A$ and a single reverse reachability pass from $B$.

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Lattice Representation (#197)"}

1. Replace each undirected link $\{u, v\}$ of cost $w_e > 0$ with two directed arcs $u \to v$ and $v \to u$ of capacity $w_e$ (or initialize a single antiparallel residual pair with `cap[e] = cap[e^1] = w_e`). Since $w_e > 0$, every minimum edge cut is induced by a vertex partition $(S, V \setminus S)$ with $A \in S, B \notin S$.
2. By the submodularity of the cut capacity function $C(S) + C(S') \ge C(S \cup S') + C(S \cap S')$, the family of all minimum $A$-$B$ cuts forms a distributive lattice with a unique **source-minimal** cut set
   $$S_{\min} = \{v \in V : A \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} v\}$$
   and a unique **source-maximal** cut set
   $$S_{\max} = V \setminus T_{\min}, \quad \text{where } T_{\min} = \{v \in V : v \leadsto_{G_{f^*}} B\}.$$
3. **Uniqueness Criterion**: Every minimum cut $S$ satisfies $S_{\min} \subseteq S \subseteq S_{\max}$. Therefore, the minimum cut is unique if and only if $S_{\min} = S_{\max} = V \setminus T_{\min}$, which is equivalent to:
   $$S_{\min} \cup T_{\min} = V \iff |S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = N$$
   (since $S_{\min} \cap T_{\min} = \emptyset$ at maximum flow).

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — ZOJ 2587 (#197)"}

#### Step 1–3: Residual Lattice Compilation & Algorithm

1. **Graph Construction**: For each undirected edge $\{u, v\}$ with weight $w_e$, insert directed arc $u \to v$ with capacity $w_e$ and reverse arc $v \to u$ with initial residual capacity $w_e$. Run Dinic from $A$ to $B$ to reach a maximum flow $f^*$.
2. **Forward Reachability ($S_{\min}$)**: Run a BFS/DFS from $A$ in $G_{f^*}$, traversing directed arcs $x \to y$ only when their remaining residual capacity satisfies $c_{f^*}(x, y) > 0$. Mark all visited vertices as belonging to $S_{\min}$.
3. **Reverse Reachability ($T_{\min}$)**: Run a reverse BFS/DFS starting from $B$ to find all vertices $x$ that can reach $B$ via a path of positive residual capacity in $G_{f^*}$. When stepping backward from a visited vertex $y$ along an adjacency list edge to neighbor $x$, you must check that the arc **entering** $y$ from $x$ has positive residual capacity:
   $$c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0 \quad (\text{i.e., } \texttt{edges[id \^{} 1].cap > 0}\text{ when traversing }\texttt{id: } y \to x).$$
4. **Decision**: Since $f^*$ is maximum, $S_{\min} \cap T_{\min} = \emptyset$. If $|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = N$, every vertex belongs to either $S_{\min}$ or $T_{\min}$, so $S_{\min} = V \setminus T_{\min} = S_{\max}$ and the cut is `"UNIQUE"`. Otherwise, any vertex $v \notin S_{\min} \cup T_{\min}$ lies in an intermediate zero-net-cost SCC of $G_{f^*}$, yielding at least two distinct minimum cuts ($S_{\min}$ and $S_{\max}$), so output `"AMBIGUOUS"`. Total post-processing time: $\mathcal{O}(N + M)$.

#### Step 4: Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (`FM-02`)

- **Toy Trace**: Let $A = 1, B = 4$ with undirected path $1 - 2 - 3 - 4$ where $w_{12} = 5, w_{23} = 7, w_{34} = 5$.
  - Max flow is $5$. In $G_{f^*}$, arcs $1 \to 2$ and $3 \to 4$ are saturated ($c_{f^*}(1, 2) = 0, c_{f^*}(3, 4) = 0$), while $c_{f^*}(2, 3) = 7 - 5 = 2 > 0$ and $c_{f^*}(3, 2) = 7 + 5 = 12 > 0$.
  - Forward from $A=1$: $S_{\min} = \{1\}$ (representing cut $\{1\} \mid \{2, 3, 4\}$, severing edge $(1, 2)$).
  - Backward from $B=4$: $T_{\min} = \{4\}$ (representing $S_{\max} = V \setminus T_{\min} = \{1, 2, 3\}$, severing edge $(3, 4)$).
  - Since $|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = 1 + 1 = 2 < 4$, vertices $\{2, 3\}$ lie outside $S_{\min} \cup T_{\min}$, immediately certifying `"AMBIGUOUS"`.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample 1 (`FM-02` — Reverse BFS Residual Direction Bug)**: Suppose during the reverse BFS from $B$, you check `edges[id].cap > 0` ($c_{f^*}(y \to x) > 0$) instead of `edges[id ^ 1].cap > 0` ($c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0$). In the trace above, when $y = 4$, the backward residual arc $4 \to 3$ has capacity $c_{f^*}(4 \to 3) = 5 + 5 = 10 > 0$! Checking $c_{f^*}(4 \to 3) > 0$ would falsely pull vertices $3$ and $2$ into $T_{\min}$, reporting $|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| > 2$ and hallucinating uniqueness.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample 2 (Counting Saturated Edges)**: Testing whether the number of saturated edges equals $1$ fails whenever the unique minimum cut consists of two parallel/series-parallel edges (e.g., $A=1, B=2$ connected by two edges of weight $3$ each: unique cut severs *both* edges, yet $2$ edges are saturated). Conversely, an extra saturated edge with both endpoints inside $S_{\min}$ does not create cut ambiguity.

::::

### Problem #198 — AtCoder ABC 285 G: Tatami `[JA]`

- **Judge & Bounds**: [AtCoder ABC 285 G](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc285/tasks/abc285_g) · Grid dimensions $H, W \le 300$ ($HW \le 9 \cdot 10^4$), cells labeled `'1'`, `'2'`, or `'?'`.
- **Untagged Statement**: You want to tile an $H \times W$ grid with $1 \times 1$ monominoes (tatami of size $1$) and $1 \times 2$ / $2 \times 1$ dominoes (tatami of size $2$) so that every cell is covered by **exactly one** tile, and:
  - Every cell labeled `'1'` is covered by a $1 \times 1$ tile;
  - Every cell labeled `'2'` is covered by a $1 \times 2$ or $2 \times 1$ domino;
  - Every cell labeled `'?'` may be covered by either a $1 \times 1$ tile or a $1 \times 2$ / $2 \times 1$ domino.

  Determine whether a valid tiling exists (`"Yes"` or `"No"`).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#198)"}

- **Target Chapter & Archetype**: [Ch 04 — Flows with Lower Bounds, Circulations & Matrix Rounding](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd) (`§4.1` Feasible $s$-$t$ Circulation with Lower Bounds `上下界可行流` on a Chessboard Bipartite Graph, also achievable via [Ch 02 §2.1](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd) compulsory vertex matching or `Ch 04` parity demand transformation).
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Dominoes on a grid always pair an even-parity cell $(r+c) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ with an adjacent odd-parity cell $(r+c) \equiv 1 \pmod 2$. Unlike standard domino tiling (where *every* cell must be matched), here `'2'` cells have a **mandatory lower bound of $1$** incident domino, `'?'` cells have an **optional range $[0, 1]$** of incident dominoes (since leftover `'?'` cells become $1 \times 1$ tiles for free), and `'1'` cells are forbidden ($[0, 0]$).

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Lower-Bound Representation (#198)"}

1. 2-color the grid into $L = \{(r, c) : (r+c) \text{ is even}\}$ and $R = \{(r, c) : (r+c) \text{ is odd}\}$. Ignore all `'1'` cells.
2. For each adjacent pair of non-`'1'` cells $(u, v) \in L \times R$, introduce a binary variable $x_{uv} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicating whether a domino covers $\{u, v\}$.
3. Each non-`'1'` cell $w \in L \cup R$ has a degree interval $[l_w, u_w]$ for the total domino flow $\deg_x(w)$ incident to $w$:
   $$\deg_x(w) \in \begin{cases} [1, 1] & \text{if cell } w \text{ is } \text{'2'}, \\ [0, 1] & \text{if cell } w \text{ is } \text{'?'}. \end{cases}$$
4. Orient all flow from $S \to L \to R \to T$:
   - For $u \in L$: arc $S \to u$ has capacity interval $[1, 1]$ if $u = \text{'2'}$, or $[0, 1]$ if $u = \text{'?'}$.
   - For $v \in R$: arc $v \to T$ has capacity interval $[1, 1]$ if $v = \text{'2'}$, or $[0, 1]$ if $v = \text{'?'}$.
   - For adjacent non-`'1'` cells $(u, v) \in L \times R$: arc $u \to v$ has capacity interval $[0, 1]$.
   - Add feedback arc $T \xrightarrow{[0, \infty)} S$ to form a sourceless lower-bound circulation network!

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — AtCoder ABC 285 G (#198)"}

#### Step 1–3: Lower-Bound Circulation Compilation

1. **Pre-filtering & Bipartition**: Delete all `'1'` cells. Partition remaining cells into $L$ ($(r+c)$ even) and $R$ ($(r+c)$ odd). Create source $S$, sink $T$, super-source $S^*$, and super-sink $T^*$.
2. **Lower-Bound Arc Table & Net Balances $M(w) = \text{in}_{\text{low}}(w) - \text{out}_{\text{low}}(w)$**:
   - **Mandatory `'2'` cell $u \in L$**: Arc $S \xrightarrow{[1, 1]} u$ has $l = u_{\text{cap}} = 1$, so residual capacity $u_{\text{cap}} - l = 0$, $M(S) \mathrel{-}= 1$, and $M(u) \mathrel{+}= 1$ (giving arc $S^* \to u$ of capacity $1$).
   - **Optional `'?'` cell $u \in L$**: Arc $S \xrightarrow{[0, 1]} u$ has $l = 0, u_{\text{cap}} = 1$, so add arc $S \to u$ of capacity $1$ ($M$ unchanged).
   - **Mandatory `'2'` cell $v \in R$**: Arc $v \xrightarrow{[1, 1]} T$ has $l = u_{\text{cap}} = 1$, so residual capacity $0$, $M(v) \mathrel{-}= 1$ (giving arc $v \to T^*$ of capacity $1$), and $M(T) \mathrel{+}= 1$.
   - **Optional `'?'` cell $v \in R$**: Arc $v \xrightarrow{[0, 1]} T$ has $l = 0, u_{\text{cap}} = 1$, so add arc $v \to T$ of capacity $1$.
   - **Grid adjacency $(u, v) \in L \times R$**: Add arc $u \to v$ of capacity $1$.
   - **Feedback arc**: Add $T \to S$ of capacity $\infty$.
   - **Balances at $S$ and $T$**: If there are $k_L$ cells of type `'2'` in $L$ and $k_R$ cells of type `'2'` in $R$, then $M(S) = -k_L$ (so add $S \to T^*$ of capacity $k_L$) and $M(T) = +k_R$ (so add $S^* \to T$ of capacity $k_R$).
3. **Feasibility Check & Complexity**:
   - Total positive balance is $\sum_{w : M(w) > 0} M(w) = k_L + k_R = \#(\text{'2'})$.
   - Run Dinic from $S^*$ to $T^*$. Output `"Yes"` if and only if $\text{MaxFlow}(S^*, T^*) = k_L + k_R$.
   - Since the network is a unit-capacity bipartite-like DAG with $\mathcal{O}(HW)$ vertices and edges, Dinic runs in $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{HW} \cdot HW) \approx 2.7 \cdot 10^7$ operations, well within $2.0\text{ s}$.

#### Step 4: Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (`FM-05`)

- **Toy Trace**: Consider a $1 \times 3$ grid `2 ? 2` with cells $c_1 \in L$ (`'2'`), $c_2 \in R$ (`'?'`), $c_3 \in L$ (`'2'`).
  - Here $k_L = 2$ ($c_1, c_3 \in L$) and $k_R = 0$.
  - $S^*$ supplies $1$ unit to $c_1$ and $1$ unit to $c_3$ (total demand $2$).
  - However, both $c_1$ and $c_3$ only have edges to $c_2 \in R$, and $c_2$ is an optional `'?'` cell with only a single unit-capacity arc $c_2 \to T \to S \to T^*$.
  - Thus $\text{MaxFlow}(S^*, T^*) = 1 < 2$: $c_2$ cannot simultaneously match with both $c_1$ and $c_3$. Output `"No"`.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (`FM-05` — Omitting the Feedback Arc $T \to S$)**: Suppose the grid is `2 ?` ($c_1 \in L$ is `'2'`, $c_2 \in R$ is `'?'$). Here $k_L = 1, k_R = 0$. $S^*$ sends $1$ unit to $c_1 \to c_2 \to T$. Because $c_2$ is `'?'` rather than `'2'`, $c_2$ has no direct arc to $T^*$; its flow arrives at $T$ and must traverse the feedback arc $T \to S$ to reach the demand arc $S \to T^*$ (capacity $k_L = 1$). If you forget the feedback arc $T \xrightarrow{\infty} S$, any domino pairing a `'2'` cell with a `'?'` cell fails to route back to $T^*$!

::::

### Problem #199 — ICPC World Finals 2007 B / UVa 1106: Chips Challenge `[EN]`

- **Judge & Bounds**: [UVa 1106](https://onlinejudge.org/index.php?option=com_onlinejudge&Itemid=8&page=show_problem&problem=3547) · $N \le 40$ grid, rational threshold $A / B$ ($0 \le A \le B \le 1000, B > 0$).
- **Untagged Statement**: An $N \times N$ chip grid has three types of cells:
  - `'C'`: a pre-installed component (must remain present);
  - `'/'`: a blocked slot (cannot hold a component);
  - `'.'`: an empty slot where you may optionally install a new component.

  After choosing which `'.'` slots receive components, let $W$ be the **total** number of components on the chip (including both `'C'` and newly placed components), let $\text{row}_i$ be the number of components in row $i$, and let $\text{col}_i$ be the number of components in column $i$. A configuration is valid if and only if:
  1. For every $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, the number of components in row $i$ equals the number of components in column $i$: $\text{row}_i = \text{col}_i$.
  2. For every $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, the row/column load satisfies $\text{row}_i \le \frac{A}{B} W$ (i.e., $B \cdot \text{row}_i \le A \cdot W$).

  Maximize the number of **newly added** components ($W - \#(\text{'C'})$), or report `"impossible"` if no valid configuration exists.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#199)"}

- **Target Chapters & Archetype**: [Ch 03 — Vertex Splitting, Time-Layered DAGs & Path Decomposition](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd) (`§3.3` Row-Column Bipartite Factorization) + [Ch 04 — Flows with Lower Bounds, Circulations & Matrix Rounding](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd) (`§4.1–4.2` Bounded Circulation with Mandatory `'C'` Lower Bounds and Slack Bypass Arcs $R_i \xrightarrow{[0, D]} C_i$).
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Two coupled constraints immediately point to `Ch 03` + `Ch 04`:
  1. Each cell $(i, j)$ independently increments $\text{row}_i$ and $\text{col}_j$ (`Ch 03` bipartite row-column factorization $R_i \to C_j$), with `'C'` forcing lower bound $1$ and `'.'` allowing $[0, 1]$.
  2. The equality $\text{row}_i = \text{col}_i \le D$ for an unknown variable load $\text{row}_i \in [0, D]$ appears to couple $R_i$ and $C_i$ non-locally — until you introduce a **slack bypass arc** $R_i \xrightarrow{[0, D]} C_i$ carrying the unused quota $y_i = D - \text{row}_i$!

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Slack-Bypass Representation (#199)"}

1. Fix the maximum allowed load per row/column $D \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}$ by exhaustive enumeration ($N \le 40$).
2. For each $(i, j)$, let $x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicate whether cell $(i, j)$ has a component ($x_{ij} = 1$ if `'C'`, $x_{ij} = 0$ if `'/'`, $x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$ if `'.'`). Then $\text{row}_i = \sum_j x_{ij}$ and $\text{col}_i = \sum_j x_{ji}$.
3. Introduce a **slack variable** $y_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, D\}$ for each $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ and enforce:
   $$\text{row}_i + y_i = D \quad \text{and} \quad \text{col}_i + y_i = D \qquad (\forall i = 1, \dots, N).$$
   Notice the algebraic magic: subtracting the two equations immediately forces $\text{row}_i = \text{col}_i = D - y_i \in [0, D]$!
4. Summing over all $i = 1, \dots, N$ yields total components
   $$W = \sum_{i=1}^N \text{row}_i = N D - \sum_{i=1}^N y_i.$$
   To **maximize $W$** for a fixed cap $D$ (which both maximizes our objective and makes the threshold condition $B \cdot D \le A \cdot W$ easiest to satisfy), we must **minimize total slack $\sum_{i=1}^N y_i$** (or equivalently give each cell arc $R_i \to C_j$ cost $0$ and each slack arc $R_i \to C_i$ cost $+1$, or give cell arcs reward $+1$).

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — ICPC WF 2007 Chips Challenge (#199)"}

#### Step 1–3: Mechanical Graph Compilation & Slack-Minimization Loop

For each candidate maximum load $D \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}$:

1. **Vertices & Fixed Supplies**: Create source $S$, sink $T$, row nodes $R_1, \dots, R_N$, and column nodes $C_1, \dots, C_N$.
   - Every row node $R_i$ must receive exactly $D$ units of flow from $S$: arc $S \xrightarrow{[D, D]} R_i$.
   - Every column node $C_i$ must send exactly $D$ units of flow to $T$: arc $C_i \xrightarrow{[D, D]} T$.
2. **Cell Arcs & Slack Bypass Arcs**:
   - If cell $(i, j)$ is `'C'`: mandatory arc $R_i \xrightarrow{[1, 1], \text{cost } 0} C_j$ (consumes $1$ unit of $R_i$'s supply and $C_j$'s demand).
   - If cell $(i, j)$ is `'.'`: optional arc $R_i \xrightarrow{[0, 1], \text{cost } 0} C_j$.
   - If cell $(i, j)$ is `'/'`: no arc.
   - **Slack Bypass Gadget**: For each $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, add arc $R_i \xrightarrow{[0, D], \text{cost } +1} C_i$. Flow $y_i$ on this arc simultaneously absorbs $y_i$ units of $R_i$'s supply $D$ and $y_i$ units of $C_i$'s demand $D$, enforcing $\text{row}_i = D - y_i = \text{col}_i \le D$.
3. **Why Cost Distinction Between Cell Arcs and Slack Arcs Is Required**:
   - In a pure unweighted lower-bound feasibility check, a cycle of `'?'`/`'.'` cells $(R_i \to C_j, R_j \to C_i)$ vs. slack arcs $(R_i \to C_i, R_j \to C_j)$ carries identical net terminal flow $N D$ from $S$ to $T$, so an unweighted circulation solver might route flow through the slack bypass arcs $y_i$ instead of placing components on `'.'` cells!
   - By assigning cost $+1$ to slack arcs $R_i \to C_i$ (and cost $0$ to cell arcs $R_i \to C_j$), or equivalently running a minimum-cost feasible circulation (previewing `Ch 17`), we find a valid circulation that minimizes $\sum_{i=1}^N y_i$, thereby maximizing $W = N D - \sum_{i=1}^N y_i$.
   - If a feasible circulation exists for cap $D$ and the resulting maximum $W$ satisfies $B \cdot D \le A \cdot W$, update the best answer with $W - \#(\text{'C'})$.

#### Step 4: Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples (`FM-03` / `FM-05`)

- **Toy Trace**: Let $N = 2$, $A/B = 1/2$, and grid:
  $$\begin{pmatrix} \text{C} & \text{.} \\ \text{.} & \text{.} \end{pmatrix}$$
  - Test $D = 1$: Since $B \cdot D = 2 \cdot 1 = 2$, we need $W \ge 2$ components so that $1 \cdot W \ge 2$.
  - With $D = 1$, mandatory cell $(1, 1) = \text{'C'}$ forces $x_{11} = 1$, saturating $R_1$ and $C_1$ ($y_1 = 0$).
  - For $R_2$ and $C_2$, the flow of $D = 1$ unit can go either through the cell arc $R_2 \to C_2$ (cost $0$, placing a component at $(2, 2)$ so $y_2 = 0, W = 2$) or through the slack bypass $R_2 \to C_2$ (cost $+1$, $y_2 = 1, W = 1$).
  - Minimizing slack cost selects $x_{22} = 1, y_2 = 0$, giving $W = 2$, $\text{row}_1 = \text{col}_1 = \text{row}_2 = \text{col}_2 = 1 \le \frac{1}{2}(2)$, and $W - \#(\text{'C'}) = 2 - 1 = 1$ new component.
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (`FM-05` — Unweighted Slack Routing)**: In the exact $2 \times 2$ trace above, if you give the slack bypass arc $R_2 \to C_2$ the same priority/cost as the cell arc $R_2 \to C_2$, Dinic may saturate the slack bypass $y_2 = 1$ first, yielding $W = 1$, failing the ratio check $2 \cdot 1 \le 1 \cdot 1$, and falsely declaring $D = 1$ infeasible!

::::

### Problem #200 — Codeforces 611 H: New Year and Forgotten Tree `[EN]`

- **Judge & Bounds**: [Codeforces 611 H](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/611/H) · $N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ vertices labeled $1, \dots, N$; $N - 1$ lines describing the edges of a hidden tree where each endpoint label has been replaced by a string of `'?'` characters of the same decimal digit length (so vertex lengths lie in $\{1, \dots, L\}$ with $L = \lfloor \log_{10} N \rfloor + 1 \le 6$).
- **Untagged Statement**: You are given $N$ and the multiset of $N - 1$ pairs of digit lengths $(\text{len}(u), \text{len}(v))$ of the edges of a tree on vertices $\{1, 2, \dots, N\}$. Reconstruct **any** valid tree on $\{1, \dots, N\}$ whose edges match the given digit-length pairs, or output `-1` if no such tree exists.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Chapter Reveal (#200)"}

- **Target Chapters & Archetype**: [Ch 01 — Conservation, Residual Networks & Max-Flow Min-Cut](../chapters/ch01-conservation-residual-maxflow-mincut.qmd) + [Ch 03 — Vertex Splitting, Time-Layered DAGs & Path Decomposition](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd) (`§3.3` Rank-2 Pair-to-Bucket Supply-Demand Network) + [Ch 04 — Flows with Lower Bounds & Circulations](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd) (Cayley Spanning Tree Enumeration $L^{L-2} \le 6^4 = 1296$ + Parent-Orientation Supply-Demand Feasibility).
- **Diagnostic Signal**: $N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ looks huge, but vertices of the same decimal digit length $c \in \{1, \dots, L\}$ are completely interchangeable, and $L \le 6$! A graph on $N$ vertices with $N - 1$ edges is a tree if and only if we can choose one **representative (boss) vertex** $r_c$ in each bucket $V_c$, connect $\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}$ via a spanning tree $T_{\text{rep}}$ of size $L - 1$, and orient every remaining edge $(u, v)$ away from the bosses so that every non-boss vertex $v \in V_c \setminus \{r_c\}$ receives **indegree exactly $1$** from a vertex already connected to $T_{\text{rep}}$.

::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Intermediate Algebraic / Tree-Orientation Representation (#200)"}

1. Partition $\{1, \dots, N\}$ into $L \le 6$ buckets $V_1, \dots, V_L$ by decimal length, with sizes $s_c = |V_c|$ and fixed boss vertex $r_c = 10^{c-1} \in V_c$. Let $\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2]$ ($1 \le c_1 \le c_2 \le L$) be the given number of edges between $V_{c_1}$ and $V_{c_2}$.
2. **Self-Bucket Edges ($c_1 = c_2 = c$)**: Any edge with both endpoints in $V_c$ must connect $r_c$ to a fresh non-boss vertex $v \in V_c \setminus \{r_c\}$ (avoiding cycles inside $V_c$). If $\text{cnt}[c][c] > s_c - 1$, no tree can exist (`-1`). Otherwise, we immediately greedily assign all $\text{cnt}[c][c]$ self-edges as $(r_c, v)$ for distinct $v \in V_c \setminus \{r_c\}$, reducing the remaining unmatched non-boss count in bucket $c$ to:
   $$\text{rem}_c = (s_c - 1) - \text{cnt}[c][c] \ge 0.$$
3. **Cross-Bucket Decomposition**: Enumerate all $L^{L-2} \le 6^4 = 1296$ labeled spanning trees $T_{\text{rep}}$ on the $L$ bosses $\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}$ (via Prüfer sequences or DFS). For a fixed $T_{\text{rep}}$:
   - Each tree edge $(r_{c_1}, r_{c_2}) \in T_{\text{rep}}$ consumes $1$ unit from $\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2]$ (if any $\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2] < 0$, skip $T_{\text{rep}}$).
   - Every remaining cross-bucket edge of type $(c_1, c_2)$ ($c_1 < c_2$), say $rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2]$ of them, must have **one endpoint at a boss** ($r_{c_1}$ or $r_{c_2}$) and **the other endpoint at a fresh non-boss vertex** ($v \in V_{c_2} \setminus \{r_{c_2}\}$ or $u \in V_{c_1} \setminus \{r_{c_1}\}$).
   - That is a pure bipartite supply-demand flow problem: split $rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2] = f_{c_1, c_2 \to c_1} + f_{c_1, c_2 \to c_2}$ so that each bucket $c$ receives $\sum_{c' \ne c} f_{\{c, c'\} \to c} = \text{rem}_c$!

::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — Codeforces 611 H (#200)"}

#### Step 1–3: Rank-2 Pair-to-Bucket Flow Network & Reconstruction

1. **Pre-Processing Self-Bucket Edges**:
   - Compute $s_c = |V_c|$ and boss $r_c = 10^{c-1}$ for $c = 1, \dots, L$.
   - Check $\sum_{c_1 \le c_2} \text{cnt}[c_1][c_2] = N - 1$. For each $c$, if $\text{cnt}[c][c] > s_c - 1$, output `-1`. Otherwise, pop $\text{cnt}[c][c]$ non-boss vertices from $V_c \setminus \{r_c\}$, connect each directly to $r_c$, and set $\text{rem}_c = (s_c - 1) - \text{cnt}[c][c]$.
2. **Enumerating Boss Spanning Trees $T_{\text{rep}}$ ($L^{L-2} \le 1296$)**:
   - Generate all spanning trees $T_{\text{rep}}$ on $\{1, \dots, L\}$.
   - Subtract $1$ from $\text{cnt}[\min(u, v)][\max(u, v)]$ for each edge $(u, v) \in T_{\text{rep}}$. If all remaining counts $rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2] \ge 0$, build the following miniature flow network ($\le 1 + \binom{6}{2} + 6 + 1 = 23$ vertices):
     - Source $S$, sink $T$, $\binom{L}{2} \le 15$ pair nodes $P_{c_1, c_2}$ ($1 \le c_1 < c_2 \le L$), and $L \le 6$ bucket nodes $B_1, \dots, B_L$.
     - For each pair $1 \le c_1 < c_2 \le L$: add $S \to P_{c_1, c_2}$ with capacity $rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2]$, and add $P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_1}$ and $P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_2}$ with capacity $\infty$.
     - For each bucket $c \in \{1, \dots, L\}$: add $B_c \to T$ with capacity $\text{rem}_c$.
3. **Flow Check & Acyclic Edge Materialization**:
   - Note that $\sum_{c_1 < c_2} rem\_cnt[c_1][c_2] = (N - 1) - (L - 1) - \sum_{c=1}^L \text{cnt}[c][c] = \sum_{c=1}^L \text{rem}_c$.
   - Run Dinic on this $23$-node network. If $\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) = \sum_{c=1}^L \text{rem}_c$, a valid tree exists!
   - **Edge Materialization**:
     - Output $(r_{c_1}, r_{c_2})$ for each $(c_1, c_2) \in T_{\text{rep}}$.
     - Output all pre-assigned self-bucket edges $(r_c, v)$.
     - For each pair $(c_1, c_2)$ ($c_1 < c_2$):
       - For each of the $f(P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_1})$ units of flow into $B_{c_1}$, pop a fresh unused non-boss vertex $u \in V_{c_1} \setminus \{r_{c_1}\}$ and connect it to boss $r_{c_2}$: output $(u, r_{c_2})$.
       - For each of the $f(P_{c_1, c_2} \to B_{c_2})$ units of flow into $B_{c_2}$, pop a fresh unused non-boss vertex $v \in V_{c_2} \setminus \{r_{c_2}\}$ and connect it to boss $r_{c_1}$: output $(r_{c_1}, v)$.
     - Because every non-boss vertex in $V_c \setminus \{r_c\}$ is attached as a degree-$1$ leaf directly to some boss $r_{c'}$, and the bosses $\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}$ form the spanning tree $T_{\text{rep}}$, the resulting $N$-vertex graph is guaranteed to be connected and acyclic!

#### Step 4: Toy Trace & Broken Gadget Counterexamples

- **Toy Trace**: Suppose $N = 12$ ($L = 2$: $V_1 = \{1, \dots, 9\}$ with $s_1 = 9, r_1 = 1$; $V_2 = \{10, 11, 12\}$ with $s_2 = 3, r_2 = 10$). Given $\text{cnt}[1][1] = 6, \text{cnt}[2][2] = 1, \text{cnt}[1][2] = 4$.
  - Self-edges: connect $r_1 = 1$ to $\{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$ ($\text{rem}_1 = 8 - 6 = 2$), and $r_2 = 10$ to $\{11\}$ ($\text{rem}_2 = 2 - 1 = 1$).
  - Boss tree $T_{\text{rep}}$ on $\{r_1, r_2\}$ has the single edge $(1, 10)$, leaving $rem\_cnt[1][2] = 4 - 1 = 3$.
  - Flow routes $2$ units $P_{1,2} \to B_1$ (connecting remaining $V_1$ vertices $\{8, 9\}$ to boss $r_2 = 10$) and $1$ unit $P_{1,2} \to B_2$ (connecting remaining $V_2$ vertex $\{12\}$ to boss $r_1 = 1$). All $11$ edges form a valid tree!
- **Broken Gadget Counterexample (Connecting Non-Boss to Non-Boss Without Boss Backbone)**: If you try to satisfy degree counts without fixing a spanning tree $T_{\text{rep}}$ on $\{r_1, \dots, r_L\}$ (or if you connect non-boss vertices to each other arbitrarily), you can easily satisfy all pair counts $\text{cnt}[c_1][c_2]$ while producing a disconnected graph consisting of a cycle in $V_1 \cup V_2$ and an isolated component in $V_3$. Grounding every non-tree edge at a boss $r_{c'}$ guarantees acyclicity and connectivity simultaneously.

::::

### 3.2 Part I Failure Mode Self-Audit (`FM-01`–`FM-06`)

| Code | Failure Mode Name | Broken Habit / Symptom | Mathematical Root Cause | Mandatory Defensive Guard & Chapter Reference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`FM-01`** | **Greedy Path Deletion & Unpruned Dinic DFS** | Finding 1 shortest $s$-$t$ path and deleting its edges (`#193`), or omitting `cur[u]` / `level[u] = 0` in Dinic (`Drill 1.1`). | Destroys the skew-symmetric cancellation arc $v \to u$ of capacity $+f(u, v)$ required by the Augmenting Path Theorem; re-scans dead residual subtrees in $\mathcal{O}(V^2 E)$. | Always augment along a residual network with `edges[id ^ 1].cap += pushed`; advance `cur[u]` by reference and set `level[u] = 0` on dead ends ([Ch 01 §1.2–1.5](../chapters/ch01-conservation-residual-maxflow-mincut.qmd)). |
| **`FM-02`** | **Saturated $\implies$ Cut Edge Fallacy & Misdirected $T_{\min}$ BFS** | Assuming $c_{f^*}(u, v) = 0$ implies $(u, v)$ is in some/every min-cut (`Drill 1.2`), or checking `cap[id] > 0` instead of `cap[id ^ 1] > 0` during reverse BFS from $t$ (`#197`). | A saturated arc can have both endpoints inside the same residual SCC or inside $S_{\min}$; reverse reachability to $t$ requires positive residual capacity *entering* the current node. | Run Tarjan SCC on $G_{f^*}$: Always-Cut iff $u \in S_{\min}, v \in T_{\min}$; At-Least-One-Cut iff $\text{scc}(u) \ne \text{scc}(v)$. In reverse BFS from $t$, test `edges[id ^ 1].cap > 0` ([Ch 02 §2.1–2.2](../chapters/ch02-residual-anatomy-cut-edges-rollback.qmd)). |
| **`FM-03`** | **Unsplit Vertex Capacities & Undirected Bridge Short-Circuiting** | Placing node capacities on incident edges (`#194`), or adding undirected edge $u_{\text{in}} \leftrightarrow u_{\text{out}}$ (`Drill 1.3`), or connecting $R_i \leftrightarrow C_j$ pairwise (`#196`). | Edge capacities constrain *per-neighbor* flow rather than $\sum_v f(v, u) \le c(u)$; an undirected internal bridge lets flow enter $u_{\text{out}}$ and exit $u_{\text{in}}$, bypassing $c(u)$. | Split every capacitated internal vertex into $u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c(u)} u_{\text{out}}$ (directed!) and wire external edges as $x_{\text{out}} \to y_{\text{in}}$ ([Ch 03 §3.1, §3.3](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd)). |
| **`FM-04`** | **Time-Expanded Horizon Traps** | Omitting waiting arcs $(u, t) \to (u, t+1)$, rebuilding $G(\mathcal{T})$ from scratch at every timestamp, or binary searching $\mathcal{T}$ without an unreachability guard (`Drill 1.4`). | Entities forced to move at every step can collide or oscillate; rebuilding wastes $\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{T}^2)$ work; disconnected destinations cause infinite horizon loops. | Always ask if entities can wait in place (`holdover arc` capacity $c_{\text{wait}}(u)$); append layers incrementally in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Dinic phases per step up to a proven reachability bound $\mathcal{T}_{\max}$ ([Ch 03 §3.2](../chapters/ch03-vertex-splitting-time-layered-path-decomposition.qmd)). |
| **`FM-05`** | **Lower-Bound Sign Inversion, Feedback Leakage & Slack Omission** | Computing $M(v) = \text{out}_{\text{low}} - \text{in}_{\text{low}}$ (`Drill 1.5`), leaving $t \to s$ active during Stage 2 adjustment, or forgetting to add $+l(e)$ / minimize slack (`#198`, `#199`). | Reversing $M(v)$ swaps supply and demand; leaving $t \to s$ open during $s$-$t$ adjustment creates an $\infty$-capacity loop; unweighted slack arcs absorb flow meant for real cells. | Memorize **In minus Out**: $M(v) = \text{in}_{\text{low}}(v) - \text{out}_{\text{low}}(v)$; read $f_0 = \text{flow}(t \to s)$, zero *both* `e_fb` and `e_fb ^ 1` before Stage 2, and reconstruct $f(e) = l(e) + f'(e)$ ([Ch 04 §4.1–4.3](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd)). |
| **`FM-06`** | **Mixed Eulerian Parity Omission & Unit-vs-Two Degree Delta** | Running Dinic on mixed Eulerian graphs without checking $D(v) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$, or setting edge capacity to $2$ instead of $1$ (`Drill 1.6`). | Reversing one undirected edge changes $\text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)$ by $\pm 2$, so odd $D(v)$ is algebraically impossible and $1$ unit of flow represents $1$ reversed edge ($2$ degree units). | Pre-orient undirected edges arbitrarily, abort immediately if $D(v) = \text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v)$ is odd for any $v$, and wire node demands $|D(v)| / 2$ with unit-capacity ($1$) arcs ([Ch 04 §4.4](../chapters/ch04-lower-bounds-circulations-matrix-rounding.qmd)). |

## 4. Readiness Bridge to Part II: Bipartite Matching, König–Hall–Dilworth Duality & Decomposition

Every technique you mastered in **Part I** serves as the direct algebraic and algorithmic foundation for **Part II (`Ch 05`–`Ch 08`)**:

1. **From Unit-Capacity Networks & Residual Reachability (`Ch 01`–`Ch 02`) to König's Theorem & Dulmage–Mendelsohn (`Ch 05`–`Ch 06`)**:
   - In `#195` (*Test Paper Library*) and `#196` (*Lotus Leaves*), you compiled matching and row-column hitting problems into unit-capacity $S \to L \to R \to T$ flow networks.
   - In [Ch 05 — Bipartite Matching, König's Theorem, Minimum Vertex Cover & Maximum Independent Set](../chapters/ch05-bipartite-matching-konig-mvc-mis.qmd), the source-minimal cut set $S_{\min}$ you extracted in `Ch 02` (`#197`) directly constructs the **Minimum Vertex Cover** $\text{MVC} = (L \setminus S_{\min}) \cup (R \cap S_{\min})$ and **Maximum Independent Set** $\text{MIS} = V \setminus \text{MVC}$ via alternating reachability trees.
   - In [Ch 06 — Grid Parity, Domino Tilings, Dulmage–Mendelsohn Decomposition & Matching Games](../chapters/ch06-grid-parity-dulmage-mendelsohn-games.qmd), the 3-way residual edge/vertex classification of `Ch 02` specializes to the **Dulmage–Mendelsohn canonical partition** $V = \mathcal{D} \sqcup \mathcal{A} \sqcup \mathcal{C}$, characterizing winning strategies in two-player walk games on graphs.
2. **From Bounded Row-Column Circulations (`Ch 04`) to Birkhoff–von Neumann & Bipartite Edge Coloring (`Ch 07`)**:
   - In `#198` (*Tatami*) and `#199` (*Chips Challenge*), you used lower-bound circulations to construct 0-1 matrices with prescribed row and column degree intervals.
   - In [Ch 07 — Birkhoff–von Neumann Decomposition, Row-Column Matrices & Bipartite Edge Coloring](../chapters/ch07-birkhoff-von-neumann-row-col-edge-coloring.qmd), you will decompose $k$-regular bipartite graphs and doubly stochastic matrices into **$\Delta$ disjoint matchings** (color classes), combining `Ch 04` degree-splitting with Eulerian halve-splitting in $\mathcal{O}(M \log \Delta)$.
3. **From DAG Path Extraction (`Ch 03`) to Dilworth's Poset Width & Hall Marriage Elimination (`Ch 08`)**:
   - In `Ch 03`, you decomposed $s$-$t$ flows into paths and split vertices into $u_{\text{in}} \to u_{\text{out}}$.
   - In [Ch 08 — Poset Chain Covers, Dilworth's Theorem, Hall's Marriage Theorem & Sports Elimination](../chapters/ch08-poset-dilworth-hall-flow-elimination.qmd), splitting each poset element $u$ into $(u_{\text{out}}, u_{\text{in}})$ turns Minimum Disjoint Path Cover on a DAG into a simple bipartite matching correction $N - \text{MaxMatching}$, while `Ch 01` cut capacity bounds yield **Hall's Marriage Theorem** and **Sports Elimination** certificates (`#200` pair-to-bucket supply-demand networks).

### 4.1 Part I Algebraic-to-Graph Compilation Cheat Sheet

When entering Part II (and later Parts III–VI), keep the following four canonical Part I compilation signatures at your fingertips:

| English Constraint / Question | Intermediate Algebraic Equation | Mechanical Graph Gadget |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Pack $K$ edge-disjoint $s$-$t$ paths** (`Ch 01`, `#193`) | $\sum_{v} f(u,v) - \sum_{v} f(v,u) = 0$, $f(e) \in \{0, 1\}$ | Unit capacity $1$ on each directed arc; run residual Dinic + positive-flow DFS path peel |
| **Is edge $e=(u,v)$ in every / some min-cut?** (`Ch 02`) | $u \in S_{\min}, v \in T_{\min}$ vs. $\text{scc}(u) \ne \text{scc}(v)$ in $G_{f^*}$ | Saturated ($c_{f^*}(e)=0$) + Tarjan SCC & terminal reachability on $G_{f^*}$ |
| **Is the minimum $s$-$t$ cut unique?** (`Ch 02`, `#197`) | $S_{\min} = S_{\max} \iff S_{\min} \cup T_{\min} = V$ | Forward BFS from $s$ ($c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0$) + reverse BFS from $t$ ($c_{f^*}(x \to y) > 0$); check $|S_{\min}| + |T_{\min}| = |V|$ |
| **Destroy / cap internal vertex $u$ at cost $c(u)$** (`Ch 03`, `#194`, `#196`) | $f_{\text{thru}}(u) = \sum_{x} f(x, u) \le c(u)$ | Split $u$ into $u_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{c(u)} u_{\text{out}}$ (directed!); route external edges as $x_{\text{out}} \to y_{\text{in}}$ |
| **All-to-all transfer inside row $R_i$ or column $C_j$** (`Ch 03`, `#196`) | Hub variable $r_i, c_j$ mediating cell incidence | Create hub nodes $R_i, C_j$ with $u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\infty} R_i \xrightarrow{\infty} u_{\text{in}}$ ($\mathcal{O}(HW)$ edges total) |
| **Edge flow must lie in $[l(e), u(e)]$** (`Ch 04`, `#198`) | $f(e) = l(e) + f'(e)$, $M(v) = \text{in}_{\text{low}}(v) - \text{out}_{\text{low}}(v)$ | Residual arc $u(e)-l(e)$; $S^* \to v$ if $M(v)>0$, $v \to T^*$ if $M(v)<0$; feedback $t \xrightarrow{\infty} s$ |
| **Equal row/column load $\text{row}_i = \text{col}_i \le D$** (`Ch 04`, `#199`) | $\text{row}_i + y_i = D = \text{col}_i + y_i$ ($y_i \in [0, D]$) | Fixed $S \xrightarrow{[D,D]} R_i$, $C_i \xrightarrow{[D,D]} T$, and slack bypass $R_i \xrightarrow{[0, D], \text{cost } +1} C_i$ |
| **Mixed graph Eulerian orientation** (`Ch 04`, `Drill 1.6`) | $\text{in}(v) - \text{out}(v) = D(v) - 2\Delta_{\text{rev}}(v) = 0$ | Check $D(v) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$; wire demand $|D(v)|/2$ and unit-capacity ($1$) arcs on undirected edges |
